newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan fisheries fear disaster as oil slicks land.
newsitem.headline: Japan fisheries fear disaster as oil slicks land.

text.p: Fishing villages in northwest Japan braced for economic and environmental catastrophe on Tuesday as oil from a sunken Russian tanker coated beaches and threatened prized shellfish beds.

Oil slicks had so far hit shore across a 100-km (60-mile) area stretching from Kyoto Prefecture to Fukui Prefecture, whose rocky coast is dotted with fish farms, fishing ports and tourist resorts, a Maritime Safety Agency (MSA) spokesman said.
"Oil has come ashore at more than seven places from Kyogamisaki in Kyoto to Oshima lighthouse in Fukui Prefecture, where the bow of the tanker has drifted ashore," the MSA spokesman told Reuters.

A 10-km (six-mile) wide oil slick broke up overnight into many smaller patches in rough seas and the first oil reached a beach at Mikuni, about 330 km (210 miles) northwest of Tokyo, at mid-morning on Tuesday, the spokesman said.
"A 300-metre (330-yard) stretch of coast at Oshima has been covered with a layer of oil," Mikuni town council official Kazuya Tada told Reuters.

The oil slicks also threaten a stretch of rocky Sea of Japan coastline on the picturesque Noto Peninsula, immediately east of Fukui. The popular summer tourist area is famed for shrimp, crabs and women divers known as "Ama".
Television showed dejected-looking Ama staring out at the choppy seas off the coast where they make their living diving for shellfish and rare seaweed without the aid of air tanks or snorkels.
Fishermen and fisheries officials predicted the slick would spell disaster for this year's harvests of abalone and turbine shell, both shellfish delicacies, and seaweed.
"Even this amount of oil will mean this year's crop will be wiped out," a fisherman said.
Kenji Ondo of the Fukui Prefectural Fisheries Organisation said he feared great long-term danger to the local industry.

"If the oil reaches rocky parts of the coast, the ecosystems could be seriously damaged. If it enters the food chain via the seaweed it could slow down the growth of organisms all the way up the chain," he said.

Intermittent snow and cold have dogged efforts to stop the oil spill -- or even confirm its size -- since the 13,157-tonne Russian-registered Nakhodka sank and broke in two during storms in the Sea of Japan last Thursday.
"Emergency boats tried Monday and Tuesday to snare the tanker with ropes and drag it away from the coast but all attempts failed because of the stormy weather," the MSA spokesman said.
"Because of the high seas we have not been able to mount a dispersal operation with detergent chemicals," he said. "We still have no idea of how much oil escaped from the vessel."

The spill, already described as Japan's second-biggest, grew worse on Monday when oil started seeping from ruptured tanks in the stern of the vessel, where most of the ship's 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil was stored.
Until the stern tanks started leaking, it was estimated that about 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) of oil had escaped from ruptured tanks in the ship's bow.
More than a dozen ships as well as helicopters are involved in efforts to stop the oil from reaching the coast.
Japan's biggest oil spill was in 1971, when 7,200 tonnes (50,400 barrels) of oil spilled from a tanker that ran aground near the port city of Niigata.
The Nakhodka was built 26 years ago and authorities said the age of the ship, which was heading to Russia from China, was probably a factor in its breaking apart in the rough seas.
The 31 crew from the tanker were rescued but the captain was still missing.
